body_markdown:
Fake beauty products have been found to contain lead, mercury, nicotine, and methanol. Discover the health risks of counterfeit cosmetics and how to protect yourself.


## Introduction


Beauty products are part of everyday life for millions of people, but new findings from Trading Standards have raised serious concerns about the safety of counterfeit cosmetics. Seized fake beauty products have been found to contain potentially harmful substances, including lead, mercury, nicotine and methanol. These discoveries highlight the dangers of buying cosmetics, skincare products and perfumes from unverified sellers.


According to a report published by Sky News on Friday, 30 October 2026, testing of seized counterfeit goods revealed concerning levels of toxic substances in several products. One skincare product reportedly contained 13,200 parts per million of mercury, while high levels of lead were detected in fake lipstick, eyeshadow and contour products.


With counterfeit beauty products becoming an increasing concern in the UK, consumers are being urged to think carefully about where they shop and what they apply to their skin.


## Dangerous Chemicals Found in Counterfeit Cosmetics


The findings highlight the potential risks associated with counterfeit cosmetics, which may be manufactured without proper quality controls or safety testing.


Trading Standards testing identified several worrying examples, including:


- **Mercury in skincare:** One seized product reportedly contained 13,200 parts per million of mercury.
- **Lead in makeup:** High levels of lead were detected in counterfeit lipstick, eyeshadow and contour products.
- **Nicotine in perfume:** Evidence of nicotine was found in a counterfeit fragrance.
- **Methanol in fragrance:** One fake perfume was reportedly made up of approximately 80% methanol.


These findings are particularly concerning because consumers may have no way of identifying dangerous ingredients simply by looking at a product.


Counterfeit cosmetics can imitate the packaging, branding and appearance of genuine products. However, their ingredients, manufacturing conditions and overall quality may be completely different.


The presence of these substances does not mean every counterfeit product contains the same chemicals. Nevertheless, the reported findings demonstrate why unverified cosmetics can present significant safety concerns.


## What Are the Health Risks of Lead and Mercury?


Lead and mercury are toxic metals that can pose serious health risks depending on the level of exposure, the route of exposure and the duration of contact.


**Lead exposure** can affect several body systems, including the nervous system, kidneys and blood-forming system. Children and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to its harmful effects. There is no known safe level of lead exposure for children.


When lead is present in cosmetics, the potential risks depend on factors such as the amount present, how the product is used and whether it is accidentally swallowed or otherwise absorbed.


**Mercury exposure** can also damage the nervous system and kidneys. Some mercury compounds have been used illegally or unsafely in skin-lightening products because of their ability to reduce skin pigmentation. However, this does not make them safe for cosmetic use.


The reported mercury concentration in the seized skincare product raises questions about the potential risks associated with its use. The actual health effects would depend on the chemical form of mercury, the amount used and the extent of exposure.


Consumers should avoid using products suspected of containing toxic substances and seek advice from an appropriate healthcare professional if they are concerned about exposure.


## Why Methanol in Perfume Is a Serious Concern


The reported discovery of a counterfeit fragrance containing approximately 80% methanol is another significant warning.


Methanol is a type of alcohol used in industrial applications, but it is highly toxic when absorbed into the body in sufficient quantities. Exposure can occur through ingestion, inhalation or skin contact, depending on the circumstances.


Methanol poisoning can cause symptoms ranging from headaches, dizziness and nausea to severe complications, including damage to the optic nerve, blindness and potentially death.


Perfumes are normally formulated using ingredients suitable for their intended purpose and manufactured under appropriate quality controls. A counterfeit fragrance containing a high concentration of methanol raises serious concerns about product safety and manufacturing standards.


The discovery of nicotine in a fake perfume also demonstrates how counterfeit products may contain unexpected substances that consumers would not ordinarily associate with fragrances.


## Counterfeit Beauty Products Are Becoming More Common


The issue extends beyond individual products. According to the Intellectual Property Office's latest Counterfeit Goods Tracker, around 20% of people aged 18 to 24 who bought beauty products in the previous year knowingly purchased counterfeit items.


The reported figure has increased from 6% in 2023, suggesting a substantial rise in the reported purchase of fake beauty products among this age group.


Several factors may contribute to the appeal of counterfeit cosmetics, including lower prices, attractive packaging and the desire to purchase popular beauty brands without paying their usual retail prices.


Online marketplaces and social media can also make it easier for counterfeit sellers to reach consumers. Products may be promoted through professional-looking photographs, influencer-style content and discounts that appear too good to miss.


However, a lower price can come with hidden costs if a product has not been manufactured, stored or tested appropriately.


## Major Raids Reveal the Scale of the Problem


Recent enforcement operations have highlighted the scale of counterfeit beauty trading in the UK.


In one raid in Bolton, officers seized approximately £2 million worth of counterfeit goods from a factory in a commercial building. The products included perfumes, cosmetics, clothing and vapes.


In a separate operation in July, the Police Intellectual Property Crime Unit and Greater Manchester Police seized 1,666 counterfeit hair products from a warehouse in Manchester. The seized items included hair extensions, shampoos and conditioners.


These operations demonstrate that counterfeit goods can involve organised supply chains rather than isolated sales.


The Intellectual Property Office has launched its Face the Fakes campaign in response to concerns about counterfeit beauty products. The initiative works with content creators and the beauty industry to raise awareness of the potential dangers.


Helen Barnham, head of enforcement engagement at the Intellectual Property Office, warned that counterfeit products may contain dangerous substances and can be manufactured in unhygienic conditions.


Independent toxicologist Rani Ghosh also highlighted the difficulty consumers face when trying to assess the safety of counterfeit cosmetics by appearance alone.


## How to Protect Yourself When Buying Beauty Products


Consumers can take several practical steps to reduce the risk of purchasing counterfeit cosmetics.


**1. Buy from reputable retailers.** Choose established shops, authorised brand websites and trusted sellers with clear business details.


**2. Be cautious of unusually low prices.** Significant discounts on popular beauty products may warrant additional checks, particularly when the seller is unfamiliar.


**3. Check the packaging carefully.** Spelling mistakes, inconsistent branding, damaged seals and unusual packaging may indicate a counterfeit product. However, convincing packaging does not guarantee authenticity.


**4. Research unfamiliar sellers.** Look for verifiable contact information, transparent returns policies and independent customer feedback.


**5. Avoid products with unclear origins.** Be particularly cautious when sellers cannot provide reliable information about where a product came from.


**6. Stop using suspicious products.** If a cosmetic or fragrance appears unusual, causes irritation or is suspected of being counterfeit, discontinue use.


**7. Report concerns.** In the UK, suspected unsafe or counterfeit goods can be reported to Citizens Advice, which can direct relevant information to Trading Standards.


Consumers who believe they have been exposed to a toxic substance should seek appropriate medical advice. Severe symptoms following exposure require urgent medical attention.


## Conclusion


The discovery of lead, mercury, nicotine and methanol in seized counterfeit beauty products is a stark reminder that cosmetics are not automatically safe simply because they look convincing.


With counterfeit beauty products reportedly becoming more common, consumers need to pay closer attention to where they shop, who they buy from and whether a product can be verified as genuine.


Saving money on makeup, skincare or perfume may seem appealing, but purchasing products from unverified sources can expose consumers to ingredients they would never knowingly choose.


Ultimately, product authenticity is an important part of beauty safety. Choosing reputable retailers and avoiding suspicious bargains can help consumers make more informed decisions and reduce unnecessary risks.

### Disclaimer


This article is intended for general information and public awareness purposes only. It is not medical advice and should not replace professional guidance from a qualified healthcare professional. The reported chemical findings relate to seized counterfeit products and should not be interpreted as evidence that all counterfeit cosmetics contain the same substances. Consumers concerned about a particular product or possible exposure should stop using the product and seek appropriate professional advice. Readers should consult official sources for the latest safety information and reporting procedures.
